methodological_rigor.justification: This population-based cohort study uses SEER-21 data covering 41.9% of the US population with over 1 million cancer cases. The analytic approach—using JPSurv to fit pre-pandemic (2015-2019) trend models and then comparing observed 2020-2021 CSS against projected expected rates—is methodologically sound and controls for pre-existing trends. Stage-stratified analyses appropriately address stage migration concerns. Use of CSS instead of relative survival during COVID-19 is justified given the absence of appropriate pandemic-era life tables. The 95% CI approach for identifying significant deviations from expected is appropriate. Limitations include potential cause-of-death misclassification (though sensitivity analysis with relative survival shows consistent results) and within-stage heterogeneity.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This large population-based cohort study (Oxford LoE 2b) provides the first comprehensive quantification of 1-year cancer survival decrements during COVID-19 in the US, estimating 17,390 excess cancer deaths (13.1% more than expected) in 2020-2021. This has direct policy implications for cancer screening recovery programs, health system resilience planning, and pandemic preparedness. The stage-specific, site-specific, and demographic subgroup analyses provide actionable public health guidance. The findings for colorectal and prostate cancers (25.4% and 16.3% excess mortality) are particularly relevant for screening program restoration.

reporting_quality.justification: The study follows STROBE guidelines and uses publicly available SEER-21 data accessible through NCI. Statistical methods including JPSurv, SEER*Stat, and R are explicitly cited. The CSS methodology, stage definitions, and subgroup definitions are clearly described. A comprehensive limitations section addresses CSS vs. relative survival, cause-of-death misclassification, and within-stage variation. Supplementary tables provide full site-specific survival data. The SEER data source is publicly accessible, supporting reproducibility.

novelty_literature.justification: This study is described as the first to examine short-term cancer survival outcomes during the pandemic's first two years in the US using SEER data. While the impact of COVID-19 on cancer diagnosis and screening is well-documented, the direct quantification of survival decrements and excess mortality is a novel and important contribution. The site-specific and demographic subgroup survival analyses extend prior literature beyond incidence counts. However, the study is primarily confirmatory of expected harms and does not introduce new methodological or biological insights.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly organized with a logical structure from population selection through site-specific analyses. Results are clearly presented with absolute survival differences and 95% CIs. Figures effectively communicate temporal trends and site-specific findings. The discussion is balanced, contextualizing findings within prior screening and treatment disruption literature. The limitations section is thorough. The clinical and policy implications are clearly communicated.

key_strengths: First population-based quantification of 1-year cancer survival decrements during COVID-19 in the US using high-quality SEER-21 data (n>1 million)
Methodologically sound JPSurv trend-projection approach controlling for pre-pandemic survival trends before comparing 2020-2021 outcomes
Estimated 17,390 excess cancer deaths (13.1%) in 2020-2021 is a clinically and policy-relevant finding with direct implications for pandemic preparedness
Comprehensive stage-stratified and site-specific analyses with appropriate sensitivity analyses using relative survival confirming CSS results
Publicly available SEER-21 data supporting full reproducibility
key_concerns: Within-stage heterogeneity (e.g., stage migration from undiagnosed 2020 cases presenting at later disease point in 2021) may not be fully captured by stage stratification alone
Cause-of-death misclassification during COVID-19 pandemic is a genuine concern, though sensitivity analysis is reassuring
Only 1-year CSS—longer-term survival impacts cannot be assessed with available data
No adjustment for patient comorbidities, treatment receipt, or specific disruptions experienced, limiting mechanistic interpretation
SEER-21 covers only 41.9% of the US population; rural and underrepresented geographic areas may have different patterns
chief_reviewer.rationale: This rigorous population-based study provides important and novel quantification of the pandemic's impact on cancer survival with clear policy implications; Tier 2 publication is appropriate given the public health significance, methodological strength, and comprehensive analysis, with minor revisions to strengthen within-stage heterogeneity discussion.
